posts.topic: 2027 capital budgets get set this quarter
posts.caption:
Building in 2027? Most owners lock next year's capital budget between now and December, and the number that goes in is the number you live with.

The mistake is guessing. A plug number with no site walk and no scope behind it either kills the project at the board meeting or comes in short when real pricing lands.

What a real budget range needs: the address, what you want the space to do, rough square footage, and when you need to be open. That's enough for us to walk it and give you a range built on actual Northern Colorado pricing.

Send this to whoever owns your 2027 budget. Then DM us the address.

#CommercialConstruction #DesignBuild #NorthernColorado #LovelandCO

posts.topic: The I-25 corridor: building on raw land
posts.caption:
Building on raw land along the I-25 corridor in Johnstown, Berthoud, Timnath, or Windsor? The building is often the easy part.

First questions on a raw site: Which town or county has jurisdiction? Who provides water, sewer, and power, and how far away are the lines? Does the site need a road, a drainage or detention pond, or an access permit? What do the soils look like?

Utility extensions and site work can cost as much as a small building. Know them before you buy the dirt.

Looking at land along I-25? DM us the parcel before you close.

Design-build in one sentence: one contract, one team, from the first sketch to the keys.

The traditional way, you hire an architect, wait for finished drawings, put them out to bid, then hire a contractor who had no say in the design. When the drawings and the budget don't match, everybody points at everybody else.

Design-build puts the designer and the builder on the same team from day one. Pricing happens while the design is still flexible, so you find out what things cost before they're locked into a drawing. SBC does the architectural design in-house, so there's no handoff to lose things in.

Save this for when someone asks you what design-build is.

posts.topic: Cold weather concrete: the 40 degree and 500 psi rules
posts.caption:
Cold weather concrete in Colorado, the short version.

ACI 306 treats it as cold weather when the air drops below 40 degrees. Below that, fresh concrete needs protection, because concrete that freezes before it reaches about 500 psi can lose strength for good.

What that looks like on site: heated subgrade, insulated blankets on the pour, heaters under enclosure when it gets serious, and a superintendent checking temperatures, not guessing. It costs money every day of winter. It costs a lot more to tear out a slab in April.

Save this if you're pouring anything between now and March.

#ConcreteConstruction #ColdWeatherConcrete #NorthernColorado #ConstructionTips

posts.topic: Five questions before you sign a lease for a buildout
posts.caption:
5 questions to answer before you sign a commercial lease for a buildout:

1. How much is the tenant improvement allowance, and when does the landlord pay it out?
2. Who owns the HVAC units, and how old are they?
3. Is the electrical service big enough for your equipment?
4. Is there an accessible restroom, or are you building one?
5. Is the space sprinkled, and will your use change that?

Every one of those can swing your buildout cost by five figures. Get a contractor through the space before you sign, not after.

Send this to the person negotiating your lease.

#TenantImprovement #CommercialRealEstate #FortCollins #NorthernColorado

posts.topic: Mistake: signing the lease before a contractor walks the space
posts.caption:
The most expensive signature in commercial real estate: the one on a lease nobody walked first.

It happens every year. Great location, signed lease, then the walkthrough finds a panel too small for the equipment, no grease interceptor for the kitchen, or a restroom that has to be rebuilt for accessibility. Now the rent clock is running and the budget is gone.

A walkthrough before you sign costs you an hour. Skipping it can cost you the business plan.

DM us the address before you sign. We'll walk it with you.

#TenantImprovement #SmallBusinessOwner #CommercialConstruction #LovelandCO

posts.topic: Restaurant buildouts: hood, grease, makeup air, gas
posts.caption:
Opening a restaurant in a second-generation or vacant space? Four items decide most of the budget:

The hood. Grease-producing cooking needs a Type I hood, a grease duct, and a fire suppression system.
The grease interceptor. Most local utilities require one, and some are big enough to need excavation.
Makeup air. Whatever the hood pulls out has to come back in, tempered, or the doors won't open right.
Gas capacity. Your line and meter have to carry every appliance at once.

A space that already has these is worth real money. A space without them needs a real number before you sign.

Save this if you're scouting restaurant spaces. Send it to your chef.
